bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Zero-debt, net-cash balance sheet — net cash of ₹271 crore as of FY26 and zero debt as of June 2026 — with healthy ROE of ~20%.
- Strong cash conversion cited as funding the strategy: EBITDA-to-operating-cash-flow at 80%, with the volume engine described as "cash-generative: scale funds the pivot to value".
- Stated sustainable dividend policy, with a final dividend of ₹3 per share (record date 7 August 2026) intimated to the exchanges.
- The 3-way demerger delivered a "uniquely defined capital allocation strategy" alongside a simplified corporate structure and clearer investment thesis.
- Growth capital is directed to capital-light, partner-led corridors and technology/AI rather than fixed assets or overseas offices.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Management's stated positioning for labour-code-driven formalisation: 'The Company's scale, compliance infrastructure, digital systems, and experience in managing large associate workforces position it well to benefit from the formalisation trend.'
- India's largest staffing and workforce solutions provider, delivering technology-driven staffing and managed outsourcing through deep domain expertise and AI-enabled digital platforms
- Low customer concentration - none of the Group's customers accounts for revenue of more than 10.00% of total Group revenue
- Diversification across four service lines (General Staffing, Professional Staffing, Overseas Business, Digital Platforms) and multiple geographies, supported by a wholly-owned international subsidiary network across Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Sri Lanka and the Middle East
- Long-standing relationships with leading enterprises, positioning the Company for niche technology hiring and integrated workforce solutions for global enterprises establishing or scaling India capability centres
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Macroeconomic and demand cyclicality — Staffing and workforce management is sensitive to economic cycles, business sentiment and hiring trends; slowdowns in manufacturing, retail, IT services, BFSI, logistics or global trade can directly reduce workforce deployment and hiring demand. Mitigated by a diversified portfolio across sectors, workforce categories and geographies and by an asset-light, technology-enabled operating structure.
- Regulatory and compliance risk (labour laws, wages, social security, immigration) — The business operates in a highly regulated environment spanning labour laws, wage regulations, social security compliance, taxation and immigration policies across multiple jurisdictions; regulatory change can alter operating models and raise compliance costs. The Company also flags potential non-compliance risk on the new Labour Codes, including incorporating revised requirements into payroll systems and increased financial exposure from changed wage structures and social security obligations - while treating the Codes as a net opportunity versus unorganised players.
- Talent availability and attrition — Growth depends on attracting, deploying, engaging and retaining workforce across blue-collar, grey-collar, professional and gig categories; higher attrition and competition for skilled talent can impair operational efficiency and service delivery. Attrition is structurally high - permanent worker turnover was 115.2% in FY 2025-26 and permanent employee turnover 50.8%, both above the prior year.
- Technology and cybersecurity / data protection — As a technology-driven staffing organisation operating proprietary platforms handling large volumes of associate, candidate and client data, the Company is exposed to ransomware, system intrusions and data breaches; a compromise could disrupt operations, expose sensitive data and cause financial, reputational, regulatory and legal consequences. Mitigations include a Cyber Security Council led by the CTO and Business IT Heads, ISO-aligned practices, periodic VAPT, DLP, 2FA, WAF, MDM and endpoint security, and a centralised network/firewall/log-monitoring architecture across offices.
- Client concentration and competitive intensity / pricing pressure — The staffing industry is highly competitive with increasing pricing pressure, evolving service expectations and technology-led disruption; loss of key clients or sustained pricing pressure can hit profitability and market positioning. Countered through integrated workforce solutions, a diversified client base, long-standing relationships and higher-value offerings such as GCC staffing, managed services and AI-enabled workforce solutions.
- Overseas business and geopolitical risk — International staffing operations are exposed to geopolitical developments, local regulatory change, visa restrictions, currency fluctuations and region-specific labour market risks across APAC and Middle Eastern markets. Mitigated by geographic diversification, continuous evaluation of country-specific regulatory environments, local operational expertise and flexible deployment strategies.
- Digital platform adoption risk — As the digital ecosystem expands, sustained adoption and engagement across associates, gig workers and enterprise clients is critical for platform scalability and monetisation; the Company relies on platforms such as Hamara HR, Hamara Jobs and TaskMo for workforce engagement and scalable service delivery.
- Operational execution risk at scale — Managing a workforce base of significant scale across geographies, sectors and client locations carries risks around deployment efficiency, service quality, productivity and execution consistency; addressed with technology-led workforce management systems, AI-enabled automation, standardised operating procedures and real-time monitoring.
- Reputation and ESG risk — As a large workforce management organisation, gaps in employee welfare, compliance, ethical practices or stakeholder engagement could damage brand reputation and stakeholder trust; workplace safety is separately identified as a material issue where failure to maintain a safe and healthy work environment may result in accidents, injuries or misconduct.

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers

business.body:
- India's largest domestic staffing player and largest private-sector employer in the segment, ranked #1 in SIA's top-100 largest staffing firms in India (2025) and #37 globally (2024); first Indian firm to join the World Employment Confederation in 2025.
- Positions itself as a tech-powered "talent infrastructure" company rather than a labour supplier — 1,200+ recruiters powered by proprietary AI technology, spanning 8 countries, 2,300+ active clients and 30K+ gross monthly onboarding.
- Moat framed around scale plus reach and stickiness: candidates sourced from 700+ districts, 70+ sourcing hubs including a centralised Center of Experience in Jaipur, 30+ offices with deep Tier-2/3 presence, and ~30% of clients with 5+ year tenure.
- Anchor clients described as category leaders — India's largest telecom operator, largest retailer, the world's largest IT services firm and largest e-commerce/logistics player — across BFSI, retail, telecom, manufacturing, IT and GCCs.
- Compliance and governance are pitched as a competitive differentiator versus the 74% unorganised/other part of the flexi market: listed status, Deloitte Haskins & Sells as statutory and Grant Thornton Bharat as internal auditors, and a formal ERM framework.
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Demerger] A 3-way demerger completed in the 2025-onwards phase reset Quess into a focused staffing play — simplified corporate structure, enhanced management focus and clarity of investment thesis.
- [Regulation] India's new Labour Code changed revenue recognition, producing a one-time revenue increase of ₹176 crore in the quarter within General Staffing.
- [Market] The India staffing & recruitment market is projected to grow from $19Bn (2022) to $49Bn (2030) at ~13% CAGR, with the flexi workforce growing 12.6% CAGR to 9.16Mn by FY27; Quess holds ~26% share of the 1.8Mn ISF flexi headcount.
- [Ownership] Promoters hold 56.9% with Ajit Isaac as founder and Non-Executive Chairman; Fairfax Financial Holdings (2013 investment) is described as the largest shareholder to date, and notable public holders include Tata Mutual Fund 7.86% and Ashish Dhawan 4.90%.
- [Governance] Board of 8 directors of whom 4 (50%) are independent, with a Non-Executive Chairman and a single Executive Director; CMMI Level 3 certified in 2026.

business.body: Quess Corp provides customised workforce management, staffing and recruitment solutions - General Staffing for high-volume talent acquisition and deployment across industries, Professional Staffing offering integrated IT staffing across verticals, an Overseas Business serving clients across the Asia-Pacific and Middle East regions, and Digital Platforms covering talent acquisition, executive search and recruitment, payroll compliance and end-to-end manpower management. The Company operates at the intersection of employment generation, workforce formalisation, compliance management and technology-enabled human capital solutions, serving sectors including BFSI, retail, telecom, manufacturing, IT, GCCs and construction. Following the completion of its demerger in FY25, the Company reports on a post-demerger basis covering Quess Corp Limited and its subsidiaries.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Three stated priorities for the next phase of growth: enabling Global Capability Centers (GCCs), accelerating the adoption of AI and technology, and expanding presence across global talent corridors
- Enable the GCC ecosystem - leverage workforce expertise and an active client base of over 140 GCCs to help global enterprises find, manage and grow talent in India
- Invest in AI across the business - from sourcing and screening to payroll, employee engagement and redeployment - to simplify processes, improve productivity and improve client and associate experience
- Build structured global talent corridors connecting India's surplus workforce with global demand, supported by expanding infrastructure for language training, international certification and compliant mobilisation
- Build deeper where India has structural advantage, expand selectively where global demand is strong, and use technology to make the operating model sharper, faster and more resilient
- Post-demerger singular focus on workforce solutions as a people-only business
- Continue to invest in people and technology, deepen customer relationships, improve productivity and maintain disciplined capital allocation
- Strengthen leadership and succession - build leadership from within and strengthen the internal mentoring pipeline; Board evolved post-demerger with independent directors bringing global, financial and sectoral perspective
- Shareholder distributions are governed by a stated Dividend Distribution Policy. For FY 2025-26 an interim dividend was paid on the equity shares and is placed before the 19th AGM for confirmation, with a final dividend for the year carrying a record date of Friday, August 07, 2026. No amount was proposed to be transferred to reserves during the year under review, with earnings retained in the business rather than appropriated to reserves. Unpaid or unclaimed dividends, and the shares on which dividends remain unclaimed for seven consecutive years, are transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund in accordance with Section 124(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 and the IEPF Rules; during the year under review there were no unclaimed dividends or corresponding shares due to be transferred, and shareholders are encouraged to review their records and claim past dividends.
- ESG philosophy 'What's good for society is good for Quess', anchored on four strategic pillars: The People Company, Responsible Citizen, Environmentally Conscious, and Trusted Institution
- Environmental: promotion of paperless operations through digital workflows to reduce paper consumption and lower the environmental footprint
- Environmental: responsible resource and waste management - segregation of paper and food waste, energy-efficient lighting fixtures, and adherence to municipal guidelines for water sourcing and disposal
- Social: mobilising talent and expanding access to formal employment, supporting the transition of workers into the formal economy with access to social security and structured employment
- Social: digital job discovery through platforms such as QJobs and Monster; vocational training, skilling and employability enhancement through partnerships and training centres across India
- Social: employee wellbeing, engagement and career development, and diversity and inclusion across workforce categories
- CSR delivered through Careworks Foundation, focused on quality education, healthcare, clean water, sanitation and community development (CSR applicable under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013)
- Governance: Code of Conduct, anti-bribery and anti-corruption practices, whistle-blower mechanism, information security and data privacy management, and continuous strengthening of cyber security and compliance processes
- Governance: Enterprise Risk Management framework aligned with COSO and ISO 31000, with enterprise risk oversight by the Risk Management & ESG Committee of the Board, supported by Internal Audit and designated risk owners
- ESG strategy, implementation and monitoring overseen by the Risk Management & ESG Committee; ESG disclosures published through the Sustainability Report and Business Responsibility Report
- Grievance redressal mechanisms in place for all stakeholder groups; all 8 shareholder complaints filed in FY 2025-26 were resolved and closed
- New Labour Code implementation identified in the BRSR materiality table as an opportunity with positive financial implication, with system and policy enhancements completed pending formal notification of state-specific rules
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The routed sections disclose no plant, capacity or physical capex programme - Quess is an asset-light workforce-solutions business and expansion is described in terms of capability, technology and geographic footprint rather than commissioning timelines. The Chairman frames the next phase of growth around three expansion vectors: enabling Global Capability Centers (GCCs), accelerating the adoption of AI and technology, and expanding presence across global talent corridors. On GCCs, management notes that more than 2,000 GCCs operate in India today and the number is expected to exceed 2,500 by 2030, with Quess already serving an active client base of over 140 GCCs and preparing to help these organisations find, manage and grow talent. On technology, the Company states it is investing in AI across the business - from sourcing and screening to payroll, employee engagement and redeployment - with the aim of simplifying processes, improving productivity and improving the client and associate experience. On geography, global talent mobility is described as one of the most significant long-term opportunities, driven by ageing populations and widening skill gaps in advanced economies against India's young, increasingly mobile workforce. No project names, capex amounts, site additions or commissioning/ramp dates are disclosed in these sections.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- GCC expansion in India is the core demand driver - more than 2,000 GCCs operate in India today and the number is expected to exceed 2,500 by 2030; contractual roles are expected to account for nearly one in four GCC roles by 2026 versus 18% in 2024
- IT flexi staffing demand is strengthening - industry employment grew 10.1% year-on-year in FY26, supported by GCC expansion, rising enterprise technology spending and wider adoption of AI-enabled business models
- General staffing grew nearly 7.9% year-on-year in FY26, with the formal flexi workforce crossing 1.9 million associates
- Implementation of the four Labour Codes is viewed as structurally positive - consolidation of 29 legacy laws, with formalisation projected to rise from 60.4% to 75.5%, favouring organised players with scale and compliance infrastructure
- Near-term headwind: Labour Code implementation affected revenue recognition in the General Staffing segment during FY26
- Near-term headwind: a softer hiring environment in certain sectors driven by macroeconomic uncertainty and rapid technological change
- Demand diversification beyond BFSI/retail/telecom into manufacturing, logistics, infrastructure, healthcare and e-commerce - bringing longer engagement cycles, higher workforce intensity, more stable demand and improved margin potential
- Mix shift from a fulfilment-led, scale-driven general staffing model to a solution-oriented, capability-led, data-driven workforce optimisation model ('from scale to smart scale')
- AI as both disruption and opportunity - creating demand for AI upskilling and AI governance roles while improving candidate matching speed, time-to-deploy and fulfilment rates; Quess has flagged AI-led initiatives in Professional Staffing
- Rise of blended gig/hybrid workforce models and platformisation of staffing services, driving demand for integrated workforce solutions and enabling scale without proportional operational complexity
- Government employment initiatives (ELI / PMVBRY) expected to improve the competitiveness of organised staffing models over informal structures
- India macro backdrop supportive - FY26 real GDP growth around 7.6%, IMF projecting around 6.5% for FY27, with services expanding around 7.5-7.8%
- Global staffing market (SIA estimate roughly US$650-700 billion) has been broadly flat for two years; Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing region at 7-8% annually to 2030
- Management flagged threats of client insourcing, macroeconomic/geopolitical uncertainty, competitive intensity and pricing pressure in General Staffing, and overseas regulatory change (Singapore COMPASS, Middle East localisation)
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Quess Corp delivered a structural inflection in Q4FY26 with consolidated EBITDA margins expanding 37bps YoY to 2.2%, driven by a deliberate portfolio shift where high-margin businesses (Professional & Overseas) now contribute 50% of profitability despite muted top-line growth. The key takeaway is the sustainability of double-digit margins in Professional Staffing (12%) and the successful navigation of regulatory headwinds (Labor Code) while maintaining a net-cash balance sheet and initiating special dividends.

risks.note: Growth depends on attracting, deploying, engaging and retaining workforce across blue-collar, grey-collar, professional and gig categories; higher attrition and competition for skilled talent can impair operational efficiency and service delivery. Attrition is structurally high - permanent worker turnover was 115.2% in FY 2025-26 and permanent employee turnover 50.8%, both above the prior year.

As a technology-driven staffing organisation operating proprietary platforms handling large volumes of associate, candidate and client data, the Company is exposed to ransomware, system intrusions and data breaches; a compromise could disrupt operations, expose sensitive data and cause financial, reputational, regulatory and legal consequences. Mitigations include a Cyber Security Council led by the CTO and Business IT Heads, ISO-aligned practices, periodic VAPT, DLP, 2FA, WAF, MDM and endpoint security, and a centralised network/firewall/log-monitoring architecture across offices.

The staffing industry is highly competitive with increasing pricing pressure, evolving service expectations and technology-led disruption; loss of key clients or sustained pricing pressure can hit profitability and market positioning. Countered through integrated workforce solutions, a diversified client base, long-standing relationships and higher-value offerings such as GCC staffing, managed services and AI-enabled workforce solutions.
risks.risk: Client concentration and competitive intensity / pricing pressure

risks.note: International staffing operations are exposed to geopolitical developments, local regulatory change, visa restrictions, currency fluctuations and region-specific labour market risks across APAC and Middle Eastern markets. Mitigated by geographic diversification, continuous evaluation of country-specific regulatory environments, local operational expertise and flexible deployment strategies.

As the digital ecosystem expands, sustained adoption and engagement across associates, gig workers and enterprise clients is critical for platform scalability and monetisation; the Company relies on platforms such as Hamara HR, Hamara Jobs and TaskMo for workforce engagement and scalable service delivery.

Managing a workforce base of significant scale across geographies, sectors and client locations carries risks around deployment efficiency, service quality, productivity and execution consistency; addressed with technology-led workforce management systems, AI-enabled automation, standardised operating procedures and real-time monitoring.

meta.thesis: Quess Corp delivered a structural inflection in Q4FY26 with consolidated EBITDA margins expanding 37bps YoY to 2.2%, driven by a deliberate portfolio shift where high-margin businesses (Professional & Overseas) now contribute 50% of profitability despite muted top-line growth. The key takeaway is the sustainability of double-digit margins in Professional Staffing (12%) and the successful navigation of regulatory headwinds (Labor Code) while maintaining a net-cash balance sheet and initiating special dividends.
